item.title: Kaspersky: BlackNevas used vCenter Host Profiles to enable SSH on ESXi, destroyed backups first, then wiped datastores
item.description: Kaspersky GERT describes a ten-day engagement in which an adversary, identified as BlackNevas from its ransom notes, used credentials taken from systems outside the virtualisation layer to reach both vCenter appliances, persisted on one with a remote-access agent and a tunnel installed as a VMware-lookalike systemd service, then used vCenter Host Profile remediation to switch SSH on across four ESXi hosts, destroyed the backup environment first and detonated a wiper-capable locker that took every virtual machine. Kaspersky states no initial access vector, victim sector or country, and no virtualisation-layer vulnerability was exploited.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

Kaspersky GERT BlackNevas case: credentials from systems outside the virtualisation layer reach both vCenter appliances, a remote-access agent and a VMware-lookalike tunnel service persist, vCenter Host Profile remediation switches SSH on across the ESXi hosts, backups are destroyed first and a wipe of the datastores detonates over ten days, with no vulnerability exploited

Kaspersky GERT describes an engagement in which an adversary destroyed an organisation's virtualisation estate over ten days: four ESXi hosts, every virtual machine on them, both vCenter Server Appliances and all connected backup infrastructure (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13). No virtualisation-layer vulnerability was exploited: credentials obtained from non-virtualisation systems inside the perimeter reached the appliances, and every action against ESXi ran through legitimate VMware management interfaces (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13). The activity is attributed to BlackNevas through the ransom notes (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13).

The attackers logged in as root over SSH to the vCenter appliance that manages virtualisation disaster recovery, fetched and deployed MeshAgent with a shell script 43 seconds later, and about four hours later returned through MeshAgent to install the Ligolo-ng tunnel as a persistent systemd unit whose name, description and Restart=always imitate appliance housekeeping (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13). They then used vCenter Host Profiles to change the TSM-SSH service state: eleven minutes after the first configuration read SSH was enabled on the target ESXi hosts, and direct SSH to the hosts then came from the vCenter appliance address (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13). Payloads went to ESXi over SFTP, a self-test of the executable ran about three hours before the final detonation, and about the first 2 KB of the virtual disk files were overwritten (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13). The backup environment fell first: the attacker extracted stored credentials after gaining administrative execution on the backup infrastructure, disabled antivirus there days earlier, then stopped backup services and encrypted the recovery infrastructure, all before ESXi detonation (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13).

Exposure
A vCenter and ESXi estate where accounts from systems outside the virtualisation layer can reach the vCenter appliances and where Host Profile remediation can change the SSH service state; the article names no version (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13).
Detection
In vCenter events and tasks and in vpxa.log and vobd.log, Host Profile remediation that changes TSM or TSM-SSH from policy-disabled to running outside an approved change window, which Kaspersky rates critical when an SSH session from vCenter or another management appliance to the same host follows within 15 minutes; on the vCenter appliance, a new VMware-looking systemd unit absent from the organisation's list of trusted services; in ESXi shell logs, execution of a newly staged executable under /tmp followed by access to /vmfs; and preserved hostprofiletrace.log (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13). ESXi logs sit in a ramdisk that is cleared at reboot, so Kaspersky says not to begin by rebooting a host (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13).

Triage: each Host Profile step is legitimate alone, so the distinguishing context is authorisation, timing, source account, change window and whether the desired state weakens security; a VMware-looking service is not malicious by default, since custom integrations exist, but one absent from the trusted list is a high-confidence anomaly, and chmod +x is ambiguous alone while execution of a newly staged executable from /tmp is itself a strong indicator (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13).

Defender takeaway
Treat the vCenter appliances as the control plane to protect: alert on Host Profile changes to TSM-SSH outside change windows and on SSH from vCenter to ESXi that follows them, review VMware-looking services on the appliances against a trusted list, and keep backup-platform credentials and administration separate from the systems that can reach vCenter, because the backup environment was destroyed before the hosts (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13).

item.title: GitLab critical patch: a merge request can reach a Git heap overflow on Gitaly; update to 19.5.4, 19.4.6 or 19.3.8
item.description: GitLab shipped an ad-hoc critical patch release on 2026-11-10 for CVE-2026-105437, a heap overflow in Git that, per GitLab, any user who can create a project and open a merge request reaches, and that can run commands as the git user with access to every repository on that Gitaly node. Git 2.56.1 and its backports fix the same flaw and five others, among them CVE-2026-111760, code execution when a malicious repository is cloned with --recurse-submodules; no source reports exploitation.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-105437 +1NATOA2

CVE-2026-105437, GitLab self-managed 19.5.4, 19.4.6 and 19.3.8 critical patch release: a heap overflow in Git's merge code that a user who can open a merge request can trigger for command execution as the git user on the Gitaly node; Git 2.56.1 also fixes CVE-2026-111760, code execution when a malicious repository is cloned with submodules; no exploitation reported

GitLab shipped an ad-hoc critical patch release on 2026-11-10, 19.5.4, 19.4.6 and 19.3.8 for CE and EE, for CVE-2026-105437, a vulnerability in Git that under certain conditions gives out-of-bounds heap writes that could run arbitrary commands in Gitaly's environment; it affects all versions from 16.2 before 19.3.8, 19.4 before 19.4.6 and 19.5 before 19.5.4, while GitLab.com and Dedicated already run a patched version (GitLab, 2026-11-10). GitLab's detection page says any user who can create a project and open a merge request reaches the flaw, which gives command execution as the git operating-system user and read and write access to every repository on that Gitaly node (GitLab, 2026-11-12).

Git 2.56.1 and the backports 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3 and 2.50.2 of 2026-11-10 fix the same flaw and five others (GitHub Blog, 2026-11-10). The one that matters on workstations and CI runners is CVE-2026-111760: a long path that passes validation is written as .git and replaces a freshly cloned submodule's .git file with a symlink to a directory that holds attacker hooks or configuration, which GitHub says can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone (oss-security, 2026-11-11; GitHub Blog, 2026-11-10). The maintainers believe it is only triggerable with --recurse-submodules and note that such a repository fails fsck, which does not protect downstream users, since an innocuous-looking .gitmodules pointing at it suffices (oss-security, 2026-11-11). GitHub Enterprise Server fixes are in 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9 and 3.22.4, and GitHub is coordinating releases of GitHub Desktop and the Copilot app with patched Git (GitHub Blog, 2026-11-10); Git for Windows 2.56.1.windows.1 addresses the issue (Git for Windows, 2026-11-10). No source reports exploitation; GitLab documents a lab reproduction in which opening one merge request left a crash entry within a second and a half (GitLab, 2026-11-12).

Exposure
A self-managed GitLab CE or EE in the affected ranges that lets users create projects and merge requests, or any Git older than the fixed releases on a workstation, CI runner or service that clones or merges untrusted repositories; applications that bundle Git need their own update (GitLab, 2026-11-10; GitHub Blog, 2026-11-10).
Detection
GitLab's rule fires when the error field of a Gitaly event contains merge-tree: signal: followed by anything other than killed or terminated, and a .gitattributes in the target branch that sets an unusually large conflict-marker-size supports a true positive; GitLab says a working attempt is silent, a clean result does not prove the flaw was not used, the rules rest on error wording captured on 19.4.1 only, and many installs do not ship the Gitaly and Sidekiq logs (GitLab, 2026-11-12). On build hosts, hook scripts or shells spawned by git during a recursive clone are the behavior CVE-2026-111760 produces.
Defender takeaway
Upgrade self-managed GitLab to a fixed release and, for a self-compiled install, rebuild both the Git in Gitaly and the Git at git.bin_path or move the distribution Git to 2.56.1 or later (GitLab, 2026-11-10); until then limit who can create projects and sign up, and on a hit treat the instance and every repository on that Gitaly node as compromised (GitLab, 2026-11-12). Servers that cannot upgrade yet can set conflict-marker-size=7 in each repository's info/attributes or turn off the merge checks for untrusted repositories (The Hacker News, 2026-11-11). Update Git on runners and workstations and avoid recursive clones of untrusted repositories until it is done.

item.title: Red Hat Quay: anonymous signing-key takeover and cross-tenant token theft; update to your branch's fixed release
item.description: Red Hat's CNA records say an unauthenticated client of Red Hat Quay can obtain an anonymous registry token, present it to the service-key rotation endpoint and install its own signing key (CVE-2026-123710, CVSS 3.1 9.8), and that an account that can create a namespace containing an underscore can retrieve other tenants' robot tokens (CVE-2026-110697, 9.9). Red Hat fixed both in Quay 3.9.28, 3.10.28, 3.12.24, 3.14.10, 3.15.9, 3.16.7, 3.17.7 and 3.18.3, lists Quay 5 and the mirror registry for Red Hat OpenShift 2 as affected with no fix, and NCSC Switzerland lists exploitation as unknown.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-123710 +1NATOA2

CVE-2026-123710 and CVE-2026-110697, Red Hat Quay: an anonymous client can install its own registry signing key and read or overwrite every private image (CVSS 3.1 9.8), and a low-privilege account can steal other tenants' robot tokens (9.9); fixed in Quay 3.9.28 to 3.18.3, no fix for Quay 5 or the mirror registry, no exploitation reported

Red Hat's record for CVE-2026-123710 says an unauthenticated client of Red Hat Quay can obtain an anonymous registry token with an audience it chooses, present it to the service-key rotation endpoint and install its own approved signing key with no expiry (Red Hat, 2026-11-11). NCSC Switzerland summarises the impact as letting network attackers with anonymous or low-privileged access read, overwrite or poison private container images and steal registry credentials, compromising the software supply chain (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-13). The condition is that the /keys endpoint is reachable by untrusted clients (Red Hat, 2026-11-11); anonymous access is on by default, and turning it off does not protect, because any valid Quay account can still exploit the flaw (Red Hat, 2026-11-13).

CVE-2026-110697 lets an attacker who creates a namespace containing an underscore match and retrieve robot accounts and their decrypted tokens from other tenants' namespaces; Red Hat says it needs no elevated privileges or victim interaction and that, where Quay is OpenShift's integrated registry, stolen robot credentials can inject malicious images into CI/CD pipelines (Red Hat, 2026-11-11).

Red Hat's page for the second flaw lists the fixed builds 3.9.28, 3.10.28, 3.12.24, 3.14.10, 3.15.9, 3.16.7, 3.17.7 and 3.18.3 and says Quay.io is already fixed (Red Hat, 2026-11-11); its CSAF record for the first flaw links eight Quay errata, RHSA-2026:99019 and 99021 to 99027, as its fixes and lists Red Hat Quay 5 and the mirror registry for Red Hat OpenShift 2 as affected with no fix available (Red Hat, 2026-11-13). NCSC Switzerland lists the exploitation status as unknown (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-13).

Exposure
A Red Hat Quay registry, standalone, deployed by the Quay Operator on OpenShift or as the mirror registry for Red Hat OpenShift, whose /keys endpoint untrusted clients can reach, and for the second flaw a multi-tenant registry where an account can create namespaces (Red Hat, 2026-11-13; NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-13).
Detection
In Quay audit logs, service_key_rotate and service_key_delete events with a null expiration_date and approved service keys nobody recognises (Red Hat, 2026-11-11); for token theft, registry pulls or pushes that do not match expected robot-account usage (Red Hat, 2026-11-11). A planted signing key survives password resets and robot-token regeneration (Red Hat, 2026-11-13).
Defender takeaway
Update to the fixed release of your branch and, until then, restrict /keys at the proxy or load balancer to trusted internal components; a deleted rogue key is not durable before the fix, because the anonymous request can install a new one (Red Hat, 2026-11-11). Where /keys was reachable, treat registry images as unverified until the keys are reviewed and, for the second flaw, restrict who can create namespaces with an underscore and rotate robot tokens of any namespace that collides with one (Red Hat, 2026-11-11).

item.title: Update: N-central: 4EverAble2Shell exploited on 21+ servers, Agent2Shell adds SYSTEM on agents; disable Legacy API
item.description: N-able confirmed via Huntress that Agent2Shell, the researcher's other chain set that gives an unauthenticated attacker SYSTEM commands on managed Windows endpoints, also needs the non-default Legacy API, and N-able has published indicators of compromise for customers that have not disabled it; N-able still has no fix, and its earlier statement that it saw no signs of compromise predates the indicators.
item.content:encoded:
Update14 Nov 2026 04:00 UTCrun 2026-11-14T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

N-able confirmed via Huntress that Agent2Shell, the researcher's other chain set that gives an unauthenticated attacker SYSTEM commands on managed Windows endpoints, also needs the non-default Legacy API, and N-able has published indicators of compromise for customers that have not disabled it; N-able still has no fix, and its earlier statement that it saw no signs of compromise predates the indicators.

The researcher's 2026-11-12 disclosure also includes Agent2Shell, which The Hacker News describes as more than ten zero-day flaws used to run commands as SYSTEM on managed Windows agents, assuming the attacker knows the target appliance ID (The Hacker News, 2026-11-12). Huntress describes it as a set of more than ten issues in how the N-central server communicates with Windows Agents and Probes, two chains of which let an unauthenticated attacker who can reach the server run commands on managed Windows endpoints, including as SYSTEM (Huntress, 2026-11-13). Huntress relays that N-able confirmed Agent2Shell, like 4EverAble2Shell, requires the non-default Legacy API to be enabled, which settles the question Huntress and Tenable had left open on 2026-11-12, and that on 2026-11-13 at 13:40 UTC N-able said it had identified indicators of compromise for customers that have not disabled the Legacy API (Huntress, 2026-11-13); the statement that N-able had seen no signs of compromise dates from 2026-11-12 (Tenable, 2026-11-12). Huntress has not observed exploitation of these issues in its partners' environments, and its Agent2Shell indicators come from static analysis of the proof of concept, not from attacks seen (Huntress, 2026-11-13). Tenable adds that N-able has temporarily deactivated the Intune integration for on-premises customers running it (Tenable, 2026-11-12).

Open finding: N-able N-central: a researcher published exploits for 33 alleged flaws and N-able shipped 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26) with seven CVE ids, but a second disclosure adds 4EverAble2Shell, a chain through Apache Axis (CVE-2026-90436) and a root escalation that works against Hotfix 2 when the Legacy API is on and is exploited on at least 21 production servers, and Agent2Shell, SYSTEM commands on managed Windows agents, with no fix yet for either →

item.title: Update: ScreenConnect SCKit: second wave hits on-prem; disable RMM+, update technician clients to 26.6.5+
item.description: Microsoft's analysis describes RelayTrap, a rogue client built on the endpoint to deliver a payload to the technician who connects, and browser-cookie routines designed to push tools through the Shared Toolbox; ConnectWise says clients 26.6.5 and later block the transfer, and a second wave on 2026-11-13 hit 205 hosts at 41 organisations, one with a self-hosted RMM+, so every technician client now belongs on the action list.
item.content:encoded:
Update14 Nov 2026 03:57 UTCrun 2026-11-14T0255Z-intelheadlinesummarytechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Microsoft's analysis describes RelayTrap, a rogue client built on the endpoint to deliver a payload to the technician who connects, and browser-cookie routines designed to push tools through the Shared Toolbox; ConnectWise says clients 26.6.5 and later block the transfer, and a second wave on 2026-11-13 hit 205 hosts at 41 organisations, one with a self-hosted RMM+, so every technician client now belongs on the action list.

Microsoft published on 2026-11-13 its analysis of SCKit, which includes RelayTrap, a malicious replacement for the ScreenConnect client on an affected customer endpoint that is designed to deliver a payload to a technician's workstation when they connect for support (Microsoft, 2026-11-13). A watcher on the endpoint enumerates the ScreenConnect client services and builds RelayTrap for each with the .NET C# compiler, and the toolkit's browser code searches Chrome, Edge, Opera and Opera GX profiles for cookies named .ASPXAUTH; a console-distribution component is designed to combine the cookie with the anti-forgery and access tokens, upload a payload, queue it through the Shared Toolbox and remove the uploaded item afterwards (Microsoft, 2026-11-13). Microsoft relays ConnectWise's statement that clients 26.6.5 and later block the transfer; in its own words the fix for CVE-2026-84869 was released on 2026-09-08 and a cloud-console update does not automatically update technician clients, and it advises live response or another out-of-band method instead of ScreenConnect on a suspected device, with connecting technician workstations in scope, invalidation of ScreenConnect web and identity-provider sessions, and no use of a cleanup script recovered from the kit (Microsoft, 2026-11-13). Blackpoint's own test found that a current Host client did not fetch or run the queued transfer, and it found no technical link between the extensions and RelayTrap or the browser routines (Blackpoint, 2026-11-13).

Huntress's update of 2026-11-13 reports a second spike at 16:12 UTC that hit 205 hosts at 41 organisations with no follow-on executions observed, one incident at an organisation running a self-hosted RMM+, a rogue client persisting as a service called Windows Update Agent, and ConnectWise's updated advisory urging partners to verify that every technician client runs 26.6.5 or later (Huntress, 2026-11-13). Blackpoint's update says the second wave appears to target on-premises instances where mitigations remain pending (Blackpoint, 2026-11-13).

Open finding: ScreenConnect: commands pushed through Run Command to at least 288 managed endpoints at 48 Huntress customers within 90 minutes on 2026-11-11 installed a rogue second client and the SCKit toolkit; Huntress links the activity to the RMM+ extension, whose versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 accepted a blank access key →

item.title: ReliaQuest: Luna Moth has staff hand over a Graph token from Copilot on a video call; no sign-in event follows
item.description: ReliaQuest reports that the data-extortion group Luna Moth (Silent Ransom Group) returned in October and early November to law firms it had extorted in May and August, using a technique it calls almost certainly new for the group: on a video call posing as IT support the attacker has the employee open Microsoft 365 Copilot, copy the Microsoft Graph access token out of the browser's developer tools and paste it to a text-sharing site, then replays it from its own server and downloads thousands of files in about an hour. The token was issued to the victim's compliant device, so no sign-in event is generated for the attacker's address; ReliaQuest is the only source and names no victim or country.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB3

Luna Moth returns to law firms that likely did not pay, with a token handoff: a video-call 'IT support' agent has the employee copy a Microsoft Graph access token out of Microsoft 365 Copilot through browser developer tools, then bulk-downloads files from the attacker's own server (ReliaQuest)

ReliaQuest says Luna Moth, also called Silent Ransom Group, has targeted law firms since at least mid-2023 and in October and early November went back to firms it had extorted in May and August; those firms appear on the group's leak site, which ReliaQuest says suggests they likely did not pay, and the group exfiltrated a second round of data (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12). The approach reverses the group's earlier flow: a blank-subject email from a free address carries a deliberately invalid PDF that crashes the viewer, and the attacker then calls the target, often on a personal number outside corporate call controls, posing as IT support responding to a "malicious email" (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12). By late August the group paired video calls with a built-in remote-assistance tool, and by October the video call alone carried both the conversation and the screen control (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12).

On the call the attacker has the employee open Microsoft 365 Copilot in the browser on a managed, compliant laptop, open the browser's developer tools to find the request Copilot sends to Microsoft Graph and copy the access token it carries, and paste the token into a public text-sharing site where the attacker retrieves it (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12). Within a minute the attacker replays the token from its own server and downloads files en masse through the Graph API, thousands in about an hour (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12). The stolen token passes Conditional Access because the device check runs only at sign-in, not when the token is later used, and, unlike device-code phishing, the token is issued to the victim's compliant device and then handed over (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12). Nothing is installed, and the video-call applications are signed legitimate software (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12).

Exposure
A Microsoft 365 tenant whose staff can open browser developer tools and take calls from outside IT, with Microsoft 365 Copilot reachable in the browser; ReliaQuest says law firms are the current focus and other sectors holding similarly sensitive data could be next (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12).
Detection
With no malware or endpoint alert, the evidence is ordinary-looking events, a blank email, an external video-call session and Graph access from an unfamiliar address, which ReliaQuest says to correlate across email, video-call and Microsoft 365 logs; a video-call screen share, a Copilot session, a visit to a text-sharing site and Graph file access from an unfamiliar address are each ordinary alone and together can indicate a token handoff (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12). Video-call platform logs, web proxy or DNS logs and Microsoft 365 audit logs each record part of the handoff but rarely reach a detection pipeline (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12).
Defender takeaway
Disable developer tools through Group Policy on managed browsers and block Graph Explorer and the browser net-export pages, because the handoff depends on users reading tokens out of browsers; pilot Continuous Access Evaluation with strict location enforcement, defining every egress address including secure web gateway ranges as a named location; and tell staff that IT will never ask for developer tools or tokens and that they should verify IT requests by callback (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12). ReliaQuest notes that default Microsoft access tokens last 60 to 90 minutes and that Continuous Access Evaluation can extend supported tokens to as long as 28 hours (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12).

Builds on: Luna Moth / Silent Ransom Group (UNC3753): vishing-to-physical-access data-theft extortion… · FBI FLASH CSA 260526, Silent Ransom Group sends operatives physically into US law-firm offices…

item.title: Update: Danfoss AK-SM 800A: six unpatched pre-auth RCE flaws, Strict mode does not remove them; France blames IRGC
item.description: Midnight Blue reported on 2026-11-11 six pre-authentication remote-code-execution flaws in all Danfoss AK-SM 800A firmware up to 5.3.2, with no CVE identifier, no fixed version and no known exploitation (BSI); CCB says updating, new passwords and Strict mode are insufficient and removing internet exposure comes first, and BSI will not rule out flaws in firmware 5.4.0 (heise).
item.content:encoded:
Update14 Nov 2026 03:55 UTCrun 2026-11-14T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagssourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Midnight Blue reported on 2026-11-11 six pre-authentication remote-code-execution flaws in all Danfoss AK-SM 800A firmware up to 5.3.2, with no CVE identifier, no fixed version and no known exploitation (BSI); CCB says updating, new passwords and Strict mode are insufficient and removing internet exposure comes first, and BSI will not rule out flaws in firmware 5.4.0 (heise).

Midnight Blue published on 2026-11-11 a report on six pre-authentication remote-code-execution flaws in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A, which it says it found within an hour of manual investigation and which affect all versions up to and including 5.3.2 (Midnight Blue, 2026-11-11). It says the exploited application runs as root, that the controller does not use the processor's secure-boot features, which makes malicious firmware that survives a factory reset or bricks a device feasible, and that the strict session-control mechanism also has at least one trivial pre-authentication memory-corruption flaw; it recommends against spending scarce effort on patching and in favour of reducing exposure (Midnight Blue, 2026-11-11). No CVE identifiers exist yet and technical details are withheld during coordinated disclosure with Danfoss (Midnight Blue, 2026-11-11).

BSI's notice of 2026-11-13, criticality 3 (Orange), lists no fixed version, says nothing is known about active exploitation and warns that the report may give attackers enough hints; its worst case is a remote attacker loading malicious firmware that leaves the devices unusable until they are replaced or restored by hand (translated from German) (BSI, 2026-11-13). CCB's advisory of 2026-11-12 relays the research, says no patches were available and that removing direct public internet exposure must not wait for them, and says Strict mode does not eliminate the risk because the research identifies a flaw in the session-control mechanism itself (CCB, 2026-11-12). heise reports that BSI told it that it does not want to rule out vulnerabilities in firmware 5.4.0 of 12 November either (heise, 2026-11-13). Danfoss's advisories page lists no advisory on the six as of 2026-11-14 (Danfoss, read 2026-11-14), and the readme for software release 5.4.0 says an update from 4.x leaves the security settings unchanged and names no vulnerability (Danfoss, read 2026-11-14). BACS's statement of 2026-11-10 that updates fix the known flaws (BACS, 2026-11-10) predates the report and does not address these six.

Open finding: Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb refrigeration controllers compromised in France, six more European countries and Switzerland, with France blaming the IRGC unit Shahid Kaveh for the October campaign; Midnight Blue reports six unpatched pre-authentication flaws in AK-SM 800A firmware up to 5.3.2 →

item.title: Elastic: CyberStrikeAI against AWS, six medium or low alerts joined only by source IP; alert on user-data bursts
item.description: Elastic Security Labs reports that between 2026-09-30 and 2026-10-16 one server running the open-source CyberStrikeAI platform used the credentials of eight AWS identities (five IAM users, three EC2 instance roles) across four accounts, reading secrets and EC2 user data and, in one case, issuing a Systems Manager command. Every step is a call a legitimate role makes daily, so six detection rules each fired at medium or low severity and only the shared source address showed they belonged to one intrusion; Elastic does not know how the credentials were obtained and names no victim.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

CyberStrikeAI turned on AWS: Elastic reads one server's 16 days across eight identities in four accounts, 56 user-data reads in 141 milliseconds, and why six detections each rated medium or low and only the source address tied them together

Between 2026-09-30 and 2026-10-16 one server serving a CyberStrikeAI web interface used the credentials of eight AWS identities (five IAM users and three EC2 instance roles) across four accounts and generated 78 alerts, the first case Elastic has seen of this tooling turned on AWS (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13). It started by validating identities: GetCallerIdentity on four IAM users in three accounts within 51 minutes, three of the calls in the same second (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13). An instance role then read a secret, made one user-data request and fired 56 more in 141 milliseconds, spacing Elastic says fits tooling working through a prepared list of instance IDs (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13). On 2026-10-02 another instance role read an encrypted Systems Manager parameter and issued a SendCommand 29 seconds later, which Elastic calls the highest-risk activity; the audit log does not show the command or its outcome (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13). After 14 quiet days the server returned and revalidated credentials, including a user in a fourth account (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13). Elastic does not know how the credentials were obtained and infers that the instance-role sessions, used from an outside address, were taken from the instances, for example through SSRF or host compromise (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13). Team Cymru counted 21 unique addresses running CyberStrikeAI between 2026-01-20 and 2026-02-26 (Team Cymru, 2026-03-02).

Exposure
AWS accounts where IAM user keys or instance-role credentials can leave the account and the principals may read EC2 user data or Secrets Manager values or send Systems Manager commands; secrets in user data are readable by any such principal and Elastic says to treat them as exposed (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13).
Detection
In cloud control-plane audit logs, a burst of user-data requests from one role session; a first-time GetCallerIdentity from one external address across several users or accounts within a minute; GetSessionToken or GetSecretValue from an instance-role session whose source address is neither the instance nor your NAT; and a decrypting GetParameter followed within a minute by an SSM SendCommand from the same role (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13). Six rules fired at medium or low severity, and Elastic recommends correlating such alerts by source address over a flexible window, since the gaps between steps ran from 141 milliseconds to 14 days (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13).

Triage: each call is one a legitimate role makes every day, so the discriminators are the source address, the number of distinct identities, accounts or instances one address touches in minutes, and the decrypt-then-SendCommand pairing (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13).

Defender takeaway
Correlate low and medium cloud alerts by source address, restrict ec2:DescribeInstanceAttribute for user data to the roles that need it, move secrets out of user data, and on a hit rotate instance-role credentials by replacing the instance profile or the instance, because stolen role credentials expire but can be reissued while the host stays compromised (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13). As of November none of the three servers served the CyberStrikeAI interface, so the indicator addresses are for retrospective hunting (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13).

item.title: Huntress: device-code phishing posing as a Teams booking skips URL reputation checks; hunt Cmsi:Cmsi sign-ins
item.description: Huntress describes a mid-October 2026 intrusion in which a spear-phish impersonating a company executive led, through a Safe Links-wrapped Google share link that sidestepped URL reputation checks, to a fake Microsoft Teams meeting scheduler whose 'Booking Reference' is a Microsoft device code, with a phishing kit shipped as AES-256-GCM ciphertext that the browser decrypts and a fallback that restarts the device-code session when MFA is required. The account had no MFA enrolled and the captured session was replayed from a residential proxy, showing as a device-code (Cmsi:Cmsi) sign-in followed by programmatic user agents; Huntress names no victim country and no Swiss link.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

Device-code phishing disguised as a Microsoft Teams meeting booking: Huntress traces an October intrusion from a spear-phish through a Microsoft Safe Links-wrapped Google share link to a scheduler page whose 'Booking Reference' is the device code, an in-browser decrypted kit that restarts the flow when MFA is required, and a token replayed through a residential proxy

In mid-October a Huntress SOC saw an employee of a construction company receive a spear-phishing email from a typosquatted domain impersonating another company's senior vice president; the link in the mail was wrapped by Microsoft Safe Links and pointed to a Google share link that redirected server-side to the lure page, so the mail body held the Google link and not the lure domain, which Huntress says sidestepped URL reputation checks for email security (Huntress, 2026-11-12). The page posed as a Microsoft Teams meeting scheduler, and behind it the backend started a Microsoft device-code sign-in; the "Booking Reference" shown to the victim is the device code, which the victim enters in a genuine Microsoft sign-in window (Huntress, 2026-11-12).

The kit is shipped as AES-256-GCM ciphertext that the browser decrypts, so that to an email scanner or crawler that does not run JavaScript the page is an encrypted blob; if Microsoft answers AADSTS50076 or interaction_required because MFA is required, the kit starts a new device-code session and restarts the flow (Huntress, 2026-11-12). After the victim finished, the attacker held a session token and the device-code login (Cmsi:Cmsi) was routed through a residential proxy; the compromised account had no MFA enrolled and was used from an unmanaged device, and Huntress contained the incident before it escalated (Huntress, 2026-11-12).

Exposure
A Microsoft 365 tenant that allows the device-code flow for users with no device that needs it, particularly accounts without MFA.
Detection
In Entra sign-in logs, a successful device-code authentication shown as Cmsi:Cmsi, programmatic user agents such as python-requests and node afterwards (often only in the non-interactive log), and a change of ASN and region inside the same session ID; in mail and proxy telemetry, a Google share link that redirects to a freshly registered lookalike domain (Huntress, 2026-11-12).

Triage: Huntress treats a device-code prompt that follows a link, a booking request or another unexpected interaction as suspicious, and the captured session shows up as a replay from another ASN and region within one session (Huntress, 2026-11-12).

Defender takeaway
Restrict or monitor device-code authentication where it is not needed, enforce phishing-resistant MFA, and investigate unfamiliar device sign-ins from unmanaged devices, new regions or residential proxy networks (Huntress, 2026-11-12).

item.title: Update: ANSSI's second REACTIV report: 64 new breaches, reuse of stolen secrets the one technique; SMS 2FA and IDOR cases
item.description: ANSSI's second REACTIV report of 2026-11-12 counts 64 further breaches, five at ministries, says all exploit the weaknesses already listed and names the reuse of stolen secrets as the technique, with new cases of an SMS second factor validated by the attacker and IDOR flaws combined with infostealer credentials.
item.content:encoded:
Update13 Nov 2026 04:05 UTCrun 2026-11-13T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarysourcessourcing_notebody

ANSSI's second REACTIV report of 2026-11-12 counts 64 further breaches, five at ministries, says all exploit the weaknesses already listed and names the reuse of stolen secrets as the technique, with new cases of an SMS second factor validated by the attacker and IDOR flaws combined with infostealer credentials.

ANSSI's second REACTIV situation report, published on 2026-11-12, counts 64 new data breaches brought to its attention since the first report of 2026-09-30, five of them at ministries or bodies under their supervision, with a significant fall in breaches detected or claimed at ministry level; it says all of them exploit weaknesses already named in September and gives the reuse of stolen secrets to reach ministry applications as the technique, which lets attackers extract the data legitimately (translated from French) (ANSSI, 2026-11-12). The new cases it describes: stolen technical accounts reused against a foreign-ministry library portal after a server compromise; an IDOR flaw in the payment API of a public registration portal for the hunting-licence exam, exposing more than a thousand people; an agent's France Travail account compromised with the SMS second factor validated, with the data of more than 60,000 agents and professionals claimed on a forum; and partner-account credentials from infostealers without two-factor authentication, combined with an IDOR flaw on a URL exposing file identifiers, which let attackers extract close to 1.2 million files from the CAF's VACAF service in three days. Education nationale is now put at 25 of 30 académies, with lateral movement over the interministerial network (ANSSI, 2026-11-12). ANSSI's recommendations are renewing compromised or suspect secrets first, systematic strong authentication, strict control of privileged accounts and tighter filtering to prevent exfiltration (ANSSI, 2026-11-12).

Open finding: ANSSI's REACTIV situation reports on French state data breaches: 99 since 1 August in the first, driven by Metabase CVE-2026-72898, infostealer credentials without MFA, IDOR flaws and supplier rebound, and 64 more in the second, which names the reuse of stolen secrets as the one recurring technique →

item.title: Group-IB: DarkLunnen's FortiOS chain leaves a 'service' super_admin; Swiss FortiGates are scan targets only
item.description: Group-IB found an open directory on a Latvian server that documents more than 14 months of operations against Europe by an operator it tracks as DarkLunnen and links to no known actor: a modified public exploit for FortiOS CVE-2024-55591 that creates an administrator named service with super_admin privileges, among other tools. Group-IB recovered a list of 4,725 Swiss FortiGate scanning targets, which it says does not confirm vulnerability or exploitation, and restic commands that accessed an S3 backup repository at a Swiss domain in May and June 2025, without naming an organisation or confirming success.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLEexploitedNATOB2

DarkLunnen: Group-IB's exposed operator directory shows mass exploitation of FortiOS CVE-2024-55591 that plants a 'service' super_admin account, a 4,725-target Swiss FortiGate scan list and restic access to an S3 backup repository at a 'Swiss domain'; Group-IB does not confirm any Swiss victim

Group-IB reports that in late July 2026 it found an open directory on a Latvian server that held the operator's /root/ directory, 457 files of which 35 were recovered, and documents more than 14 months of operations against Europe by an operator it tracks as DarkLunnen; Group-IB links it to no known actor and does not establish nationality or state affiliation (Group-IB, 2026-11-11). The main campaign used a modified watchTowr proof of concept for FortiOS CVE-2024-55591, designed to create a backdoor super-admin account named service (Group-IB, 2026-11-11); the recovered results list about 600 devices in Turkey (hospitals, industry and municipalities), 16 in Ukraine, 14 in Azerbaijan and 1 in Algeria, and a stolen FortiGate configuration from a Romanian organisation carried the same account and yielded 10 cleartext VPN passwords (Group-IB, 2026-11-11).

The Swiss content is thin. Group-IB recovered a list of 4,725 FortiGate scanning targets for Switzerland and says such lists identify scanning targets but do not confirm vulnerability or successful exploitation; a table of additional operations also lists restic commands with AWS credentials accessing an S3 repository at a Swiss domain in May and June 2025, with production snapshots enumerated, and the report names no organisation and says that for several operations the evidence is limited to recorded commands (Group-IB, 2026-11-11). Fortinet's advisory FG-IR-24-535 lists FortiOS 7.0.0 through 7.0.16 and FortiProxy 7.2.0 through 7.2.12 and 7.0.0 through 7.0.19 as affected, fixed in 7.0.17, 7.2.13 and 7.0.20, names FortiOS 7.2, 7.4, 7.6 and 6.4 as not affected and offers disabling the HTTP/HTTPS administrative interface as the workaround (Fortinet PSIRT, 2025-01-14).

Exposure
A FortiOS 7.0 device below 7.0.17, or a FortiProxy below its fixed release, whose HTTP/HTTPS administrative interface was ever reachable from the internet; a device exposed while vulnerable can carry an account that patching does not remove (Group-IB, 2026-11-11).
Detection
In FortiGate event logs, an administrator named service with the super_admin profile, any unexplained administrator or local user, and super_admin logins or account creation through the jsconsole interface, which Fortinet lists among its indicators; in VPN logs, logins with accounts whose secrets sat in an exposed configuration (Group-IB, 2026-11-11).
Defender takeaway
Hunt for the account on patched devices too, assume the configuration was read on a device that was exposed while vulnerable and rotate the VPN user passwords, administrator passwords, IPsec pre-shared keys and LDAP or RADIUS credentials it stored, review VPN logs and enforce MFA, and enable private data encryption, which is off by default (Group-IB, 2026-11-11); no source says that a Swiss organisation was compromised.

item.title: WFX Phantom: stolen GitHub tokens push a CI stealer; cloud persistence meant to survive rotation; check for probe PRs
item.description: StepSecurity and Aikido report that from 2026-11-10 an attacker uses stolen GitHub tokens, not a GitHub Actions bug, to open probe pull requests titled "docs: dependency audit notes" and then push a stealer script into workflows, CI scripts or npm hooks where the token's permissions allow, taking Actions secrets, runner memory and cloud credentials, planting AWS and Azure persistence and deleting the workflow runs. Counts differ by lab and time (more than 63,000 probes; at least 1,835 repositories where the payload ran); how the tokens were obtained is unknown, and no Swiss victim is named.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB1

WFX Phantom: stolen GitHub tokens push a CI secret stealer into repositories from 2026-11-10, steal Actions secrets, runner memory and cloud tokens, plant AWS and Azure persistence designed to outlast rotation and delete the workflow runs; StepSecurity counts more than 63,000 probe pull requests

StepSecurity reports that from 2026-11-10 an attacker uses stolen GitHub tokens of real developer and bot accounts, as a developer would, not a bug in GitHub Actions, to push a CI secret stealer into repositories those tokens can write to (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12). It first opens a pull request titled "docs: dependency audit notes" from a branch named wfx-docs that only proves write access; StepSecurity counts more than 63,000 such probes by 2026-11-12 (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12), Aikido, which tracks the campaign as wfx-loot, counts 4,837 compromised accounts and at least 1,835 repositories where the payload ran, and Endor Labs counts 8,926 infected repositories (Aikido, 2026-11-12; Endor Labs, 2026-11-12); BleepingComputer reports that the compromised accounts included those of the US General Services Administration and the French government (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-12).

Where the token's permissions and the repository's setup let it run, the attacker pushes a script of about 1,500 lines through an edit to an existing workflow or CI shell script, a new workflow on a short-lived branch or a hidden script that an npm hook runs, and the script collects every Actions secret, the job token, the memory of the runner worker process and credential files for the major clouds and registries, then uses the job's OIDC token to open AWS, GCP and Azure sessions (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12). It plants persistence meant to outlast rotation, a rewritten AWS role trust policy with new access keys and federated identity credentials on Azure applications, sends the archive over HTTP and from 2026-11-12 through a Telegram bot, and within about a minute pushes a revert commit and deletes the workflow run, leaving a gap in the run numbers that StepSecurity calls the most reliable sign the stealer ran (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12). How the tokens were obtained is not known: some probes came through the Fly.io GitHub App, and StepSecurity has no evidence of a breach of Fly.io (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12). BleepingComputer's report of Aikido's findings gives the same probe title and start date (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-12).

Exposure
Any account or bot with write access to repositories you own or build from whose token may be exposed (a personal access token, an OAuth grant, a GitHub App user token), and any build with cloud OIDC trust or long-lived secrets; bots that bypass branch protection raise the risk (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12).
Detection
In source-control data, pull requests titled "docs: dependency audit notes", branches named wfx-docs and commits since 2026-11-10 with the messages "ci: refresh build cache", "ci: restore", "ci: cleanup", "chore: add ci helper" or "chore: add dependency audit workflow", and in CI run history a gap in the run numbers right after one; in AWS and Azure audit logs, changes to role trust policies, newly created access keys and federated credentials named wfx-ci (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12).

Triage: a probe pull request alone shows that the account that opened it is compromised, even if nothing else happened; the payload probably ran where a commit with one of those messages is paired with a deleted run (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12).

Defender takeaway
Treat the account behind any probe or payload commit as compromised and revoke its tokens; where the payload ran, rotation is not enough because the persistence is designed to outlast it, and Endor Labs says secrets rotated after the first wave were likely stolen again in 1,838 repositories (Endor Labs, 2026-11-12).

item.title: SignDrop: public Windows LPE to SYSTEM through CLFS and Defender; no CVE or patch; check CLFS authentication Mode
item.description: Cyderes Howler Cell reproduced SignDrop, a Windows local privilege escalation from a standard user to SYSTEM that was published on GitHub on 2026-11-10, the day of Patch Tuesday, with no coordinated disclosure, no CVE and no patch. It makes Defender's signature-update RPC and symbolic links get clfs.sys to write a SYSTEM-owned authentication file where the attacker chooses, so it applies where the CLFS authentication Mode is 0 or 1; no exploitation is reported, Microsoft has not commented, and the researcher's claim that about 80% of Windows installations are exposed is unsubstantiated.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

SignDrop: a public Windows local privilege escalation to SYSTEM that turns Microsoft's CLFS authentication mitigation against itself through Defender's signature-update RPC; proof of concept published 2026-11-10, no CVE and no patch, no exploitation reported

Cyderes Howler Cell reports that the exploit was published on 2026-11-10 under a GitHub handle, the same day as November Patch Tuesday, with no coordinated disclosure, no CVE and no patch, and that its team reproduced a SYSTEM shell from a standard user session (Cyderes, 2026-11-12). The chain is a logic bug with no memory corruption: CLFS containers are created through Object Manager symbolic links, an oplock on a bait file confirms that Microsoft Defender has engaged, a call to Defender's signature-update RPC makes clfs.sys create its .cnpf authentication-signature file as SYSTEM at an attacker-chosen path, here hid.dll in the Common Files\microsoft shared\ink directory, a file that does not ship in that directory; the content is replaced with a payload DLL and a runas request makes consent.exe load it, which starts a SYSTEM conhost.exe on the user's desktop (Cyderes, 2026-11-12). Like every release of the same cluster it needs a foothold on the host first. It applies where the CLFS authentication Mode value, under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication, is 0 or 1 (Cyderes, 2026-11-12).

Cyderes says the feature ships enabled on current Windows versions and that the researcher tested Windows 11 26H2 and experimental builds of Windows 11 and Windows Server 2025; the researcher's estimate that 80% of Windows installations are vulnerable has no data behind it (Cyderes, 2026-11-12). The researcher adds that, because the privileged file creation appears to come from the antimalware engine's own process, the technique can be used against any antimalware engine's self-defense; that claim rests on his statement alone (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-12). No source reports exploitation, and Microsoft had not commented publicly as of 2026-11-11 (SecurityOnline, 2026-11-11).

Exposure
Any Windows host on which an attacker can already run code as a standard user and whose CLFS authentication Mode is 0 or 1; Cyderes tells defenders to read the Mode value on every host to size the population (Cyderes, 2026-11-12).
Detection
File-creation telemetry for hid.dll in the ink directory, which Cyderes counts, with the Defender signature-update RPC call, among its two highest-signal observables because the file does not ship in that directory; that RPC called from a process outside the Defender service tree; symbolic-link churn under \BaseNamedObjects\Restricted\ correlated with Defender RPC activity; consent.exe loading a DLL from the ink directory; and a SYSTEM conhost.exe on the interactive desktop right after a hid.dll write. The exploit deletes hid.dll afterwards, so keep file-creation and image-load telemetry rather than relying on a disk sweep (Cyderes, 2026-11-12).

Triage: Cyderes calls a hid.dll creation in the ink directory and a Defender signature-update RPC from outside the Defender service tree rare enough in a typical estate to alert on rather than hunt, and the first is a successful write whatever the variant (Cyderes, 2026-11-12).

Defender takeaway
No patch exists, so inventory the Mode value, restrict untrusted local code execution with application and script control, and do not switch CLFS authentication off as a workaround, because that re-exposes the older memory-corruption attacks it blocks; Cyderes counts sixteen public releases from the same researcher in roughly thirty-one weeks, so expect more (Cyderes, 2026-11-12).

item.title: XWEB EVO refrigeration controllers: 14 CVEs, unauthenticated root RCE and a hard-coded password, no fix will ship
item.description: VulnCheck, as CNA, published 14 CVEs on 2026-11-12 for XWEB EVO, the end-of-service Copeland and Dixell web supervisor for refrigeration and cold-chain equipment, seven of them scored CVSS 4.0 9.2 to 9.3: unauthenticated command injection that runs as root, a hard-coded Administrator password, and Administrator and root passwords computed from the device MAC address and date. Copeland ended software support on 2026-03-16 and ships no security fixes, and on 2026-10-14 it told operators to remove all XWEB EVO units from the public internet; no source reports exploitation of these CVEs or ties them to the refrigeration attacks that French and Swiss authorities warn about.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-124007 +6NATOB2

Dixell/Copeland XWEB EVO refrigeration supervisors: VulnCheck published 14 CVEs on 2026-11-12, seven scored CVSS 4.0 9.2 to 9.3 (unauthenticated command injection that runs as root, a hard-coded Administrator password, Administrator and root passwords computed from the MAC address and date); Copeland ended support on 2026-03-16 and ships no fixes; no exploitation reported

VulnCheck, the assigning CNA, describes unauthenticated command injection in XWEB EVO through the password field (VulnCheck, 2026-11-12) and the username field (VulnCheck, 2026-11-12) of its login and API scripts, and through the sh parameter of the setuid xwconsole.cgi (VulnCheck, 2026-11-12), all reaching root; a hard-coded password for the built-in Administrator account that gives a full session in one request (VulnCheck, 2026-11-12); and Administrator and root passwords that can be computed offline from the device MAC address and the date (VulnCheck, 2026-11-12; VulnCheck, 2026-11-12; VulnCheck, 2026-11-12). The cluster holds 14 records, and the seven scored 9.2 or higher are the ones covered here (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-12). The records' ranges end before 5.6.2 or 5.7.0 or run through 5.8.8, but Copeland's download pages list EVO packages only up to 5.2.3 of 2018 (Copeland, 2026-11-13), and its bulletin says software support ended on 2026-03-16 with no further firmware or security updates (Copeland, 2026-03-16), so no source shows where a fixed build can be had.

No source reports exploitation or a public proof of concept for these CVEs, and none ties them to the compromises of Danfoss, Copeland and Dixell controllers. Copeland's bulletin of 2026-10-14, carried in the Dixell France guide that CERT-FR links, acknowledges a vulnerability on an end-of-life generation of XWEB EVO controllers and tells operators to remove all XWEB EVO units from the public internet immediately (translated from French) (Dixell France, 2026-10-14); NCSC Switzerland says that guidance addresses end-of-service XWEB EVO systems and that the public information does not confirm exploitation of the Danfoss CVEs it lists (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-06), and BACS lists Copeland and Dixell XWEB as potentially affected (BACS, 2026-11-10). The one compromised-unit log read concerns an XWEB Pro, not an EVO (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-06).

Exposure
An XWEB EVO unit, sold until October 2023 (Copeland, 2026-03-16), whose login page appears when the site's public address is opened from outside the site network, which is the vendor's own test (Dixell France, 2026-10-14).
Detection
No source gives log artefacts for these flaws. After suspected access the vendor's procedure is to review the user list and profiles and the alarm categories, levels and recipients with a test alarm, and to read product temperatures directly in the cabinets because setpoints or alarm thresholds may have changed; CERT-FR says a factory reset removes persistence but leaves an end-of-life unit vulnerable (Dixell France, 2026-10-14; CERT-FR, 2026-10-16).
Defender takeaway
No fix is coming, so keep XWEB EVO units off the internet and reach them only through a VPN, and plan the move to the supported XWEB Pro (Dixell France, 2026-10-14).

item.title: PTC Windchill and FlexPLM: new unauthenticated deserialization RCE patched 11 Nov; fixed releases behind PTC login
item.description: PTC's CNA record, restated by NCSC Switzerland and BSI, says CVE-2026-126325 lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker run code on PTC Windchill and FlexPLM through deserialization of untrusted data (CVSS 4.0 9.2, high attack complexity), in eleven Windchill and ten FlexPLM release lines. PTC announced a patch on 2026-11-11 (its advisory sits behind a customer login, so no fixed release is public) and has already patched PTC-hosted environments; no source reports exploitation of this flaw, although CISA listed an earlier Windchill and FlexPLM RCE as exploited in June.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-126325NATOA2

CVE-2026-126325, PTC Windchill and FlexPLM: deserialization of untrusted data lets an unauthenticated remote attacker run code (CVSS 4.0 9.2, high attack complexity); PTC announced a patch on 2026-11-11 and keeps the fixed releases behind its support login, no exploitation is reported, and an earlier Windchill flaw was exploited in June

PTC's CNA record, published on 2026-11-11, describes CVE-2026-126325 as a critical remote code execution flaw in PTC Windchill and PTC FlexPLM that may be exploited through the deserialization of untrusted data, scored CVSS 4.0 9.2 with high attack complexity, no privileges and no user interaction (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-11). NCSC Switzerland says successful exploitation lets remote attackers achieve code execution and potentially full system compromise through crafted network requests carrying malicious serialized data, with network access to the exposed system as the prerequisite (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-12); BSI describes a remote, anonymous attacker (translated from German) (BSI CERT-Bund, 2026-11-11). The affected release lines are Windchill 11.0 M030, 11.1 M020, 11.2.1.0, 12.0.2.0, 12.1.2.0, 13.0.2.0 and 13.1.0.0 to 13.1.4.0, with ten FlexPLM releases up to 13.1.3.0 (The Hacker News, 2026-11-12).

PTC's Trust Center says a patch has been available since 2026-11-11, that a Windchill administrator applies it, that PTC-hosted environments were patched on the customer's behalf, and that self-hosted customers are urged to apply it as soon as possible (PTC Trust Center, 2026-11-11). The vendor advisory sits behind a customer login, so no fixed release is public (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-12). NCSC Switzerland lists the exploitation status as unknown (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-12), and PTC's change log records no attack on this flaw (PTC Trust Center, 2026-11-11). The product has a history: CISA listed the earlier Windchill and FlexPLM flaw CVE-2026-12569 as exploited in June (The Hacker News, 2026-06-26), and Ransom-ISAC, eCrime.ch and DEFUSED reported Cl0p-linked attackers chaining a FlexPLM information disclosure with a Windchill login-servlet flaw to drop JSP web shells (The Hacker News, 2026-07-25).

Exposure
A self-hosted Windchill or FlexPLM server on one of the listed release lines that a hostile network can reach; PTC-hosted environments need no action (PTC Trust Center, 2026-11-11).
Detection
No source gives a detection for this flaw. For the June intrusions PTC told readers to search access logs for POST requests to /Windchill/login/ JSP files, which legitimate traffic does not make, and to look for persistent JSP web shells in the Windchill login directory (PTC Trust Center, 2026-11-11); whether the same pattern applies to CVE-2026-126325 is not stated.
Defender takeaway
Patch self-hosted Windchill and FlexPLM now, internet-reachable servers first, and ask PTC for the fixed release of your line through the support portal, because no fixed version is public (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-12).

item.title: NetScaler: 28 flaws fixed, one reaches every default ADC and Gateway; update to 14.1-73.57 or 13.1-64.39
item.description: Cloud Software Group's bulletin CTX697305 of 2026-11-12 fixes 28 flaws in customer-managed NetScaler ADC and Gateway, 9 of them scored CVSS 4.0 9.0 or above; CVE-2026-120868 (9.3) needs no feature or authentication and affects every deployment in default configuration, and CVE-2026-107412 (9.5) reaches Gateway and AAA virtual servers. The fixed builds are 14.1-73.57, 13.1-64.39, 14.1-73.58 FIPS and 13.1-37.293, and bulletin CTX697320 fixes an unauthenticated NetScaler Console authentication bypass in 14.1-74.34; the bulletins describe the impact as unpredictable behaviour or denial of service, offer no workaround and state no exploitation status, while CERT-EU writes that Citrix reports none and no source reports an attack.
item.content:encoded:
HIGHCVE-2026-120868 +28NATOA2

Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway: 28 flaws fixed on 2026-11-12, among them CVE-2026-120868 (CVSS 4.0 9.3) in packet processing on every deployment in default configuration, plus an unauthenticated NetScaler Console authentication bypass (CVE-2026-120869); no exploitation reported

Cloud Software Group's bulletin CTX697305 of 2026-11-12 fixes 28 flaws in customer-managed NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway (Cloud Software Group, 2026-11-12). The bulletin describes the impact as unpredictable or erroneous behaviour or denial of service, while its CVSS 4.0 vectors score confidentiality, integrity and availability impact High on ten rows, and no source says that code execution is possible (CERT-EU, 2026-11-12). The row that applies everywhere is CVE-2026-120868 (9.3), a memory overflow in packet processing with the precondition "All NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway deployments (Default configuration / No additional feature required)" and no authentication or user interaction (Cloud Software Group, 2026-11-12). CVE-2026-107412 (9.5) covers several overflows on an appliance configured as a Gateway (SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN or RDP Proxy) or an AAA virtual server, which CERT-EU, citing the vendor, says can be reached without authentication (CERT-EU, 2026-11-12); further rows at 9.3 or 8.7 each depend on one configured feature, such as an SMPP, DNS-over-HTTPS or PUSH virtual server or a SAML, WebAuth, email OTP, certificate or LDAP authentication action, and CVE-2026-120863 needs only a path from an untrusted host to the management address NSIP or NSIP6 (Cloud Software Group, 2026-11-12). Bulletin CTX697320 fixes CVE-2026-120869, an unauthenticated authentication bypass on the NetScaler Console, scored 9.4 with an adjacent vector in the bulletin (Cloud Software Group, 2026-11-12) and 9.3 with a network vector in ENISA's record (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-12).

The fixed builds are 14.1-73.57, 13.1-64.39, 14.1-73.58 FIPS and 13.1-37.293 for 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP (Cloud Software Group, 2026-11-12), and 14.1-74.34 for the Console (Cloud Software Group, 2026-11-12); Secure Private Access Hybrid deployments must upgrade their NetScaler instances (Cloud Software Group, 2026-11-12). Neither bulletin states an exploitation status or a workaround. CERT-EU writes that Citrix reports no exploitation and no confirmed public proof of concept (CERT-EU, 2026-11-12), NCSC Switzerland lists the exploitation status as unknown (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-12), and none of the CVEs is in CISA's catalog. heise reports that Citrix will publish NetScaler security fixes monthly on a fixed date close to Patch Tuesday from now on, with out-of-cycle updates for urgent cases such as active exploitation (heise, 2026-11-12).

Exposure
Every customer-managed NetScaler ADC or Gateway below the fixed build of its branch is in scope for CVE-2026-120868 whatever its configuration; the other rows apply where the named feature is configured, which the bulletin tells you to find with configuration searches such as add vpn vserver, add authentication vserver or add authentication samlAction (Cloud Software Group, 2026-11-12).
Detection
No source states a detection method or a check for compromise. The stated impact is a crash or denial of service, so unexplained packet-engine restarts, core files or reboots after inbound traffic to a Gateway or AAA virtual server are the telemetry to review; this is an inference, not a source statement. Where a logout had occurred, /var/log/httperror.log can hold authentication material (one of the rows), so limit who can read that file (Cloud Software Group, 2026-11-12).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade internet-facing Gateway and AAA appliances first, then every other ADC, to the fixed build of the branch, because CVE-2026-120868 needs no feature (CERT-EU, 2026-11-12) and neither bulletin offers a workaround (Cloud Software Group, 2026-11-12; Cloud Software Group, 2026-11-12); keep NSIP and the Console IP on a management network.

Check Point Research reports that exploitation of unpatched Check Point gateways began on 2026-10-30 and says it escalated to root with a second flaw, CVE-2026-123039, which Check Point rates CVSS 7.8 and says it saw exploited against a couple of dozen customers (Check Point Research, 2026-11-12; Check Point, 2026-11-12). Open finding: CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619 and CVE-2026-123039, Check Point Force, Spark and Cloud firewalls: PHP2Shell on the Mobile Access and VPN web interfaces, chained with a local root escalation, is exploited against unpatched gateways (implant, ESXi wiper); the fix is in Jumbo takes R81.20 take 174, R82 take 132, R82.10 take 52 and R82.20 take 14 →

item.title: Update: eMudhra: eight ECDSA CA keys guessable, eight RSA CAs revoked; Windows drops the rest 2026-11-16; update clients
item.description: eMudhra's full incident report of 2026-11-10 says eight RSA-4096 issuers (G2B and G2C) were revoked on 2026-11-07 with the reason cessationOfOperation because their keys were handled in the memory of a Python script, so eMudhra cannot show compliance with its policy; it had said on 2026-10-19 that they were not impacted, no source says the keys leaked, and the G2C issuers had issued end-entity certificates.
item.content:encoded:
Update12 Nov 2026 04:26 UTCrun 2026-11-12T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

eMudhra's full incident report of 2026-11-10 says eight RSA-4096 issuers (G2B and G2C) were revoked on 2026-11-07 with the reason cessationOfOperation because their keys were handled in the memory of a Python script, so eMudhra cannot show compliance with its policy; it had said on 2026-10-19 that they were not impacted, no source says the keys leaked, and the G2C issuers had issued end-entity certificates.

eMudhra posted its full incident report in the Mozilla bug on 2026-11-10 (eMudhra, Mozilla bug 2083449, 2026-11-10). For the eight RSA-4096 issuers (G2B and G2C) it says the key integrity is intact, all signatures verifying, but that during re-import the private-key material was handled in the volatile memory of a Python process on the ceremony host, which is not consistent with its certification practice statement, so the RSA issuers are treated as not meeting it; it adds that logs cannot reliably establish or exclude how that material was handled (eMudhra, Mozilla bug 2083449, 2026-11-10). It identified this in early November after a root-program discussion, revoked the eight issuers on 2026-11-07 with the reason cessationOfOperation, not the compromise reason used for the ECDSA set, and had written on 2026-10-19 that the RSA issuers were not impacted (eMudhra, Mozilla bug 2083449, 2026-11-10; eMudhra, Mozilla bug 2083449, 2026-10-19). The G2C issuers were put into production in May 2026 and issued end-entity certificates, the last on 2026-11-03, after which issuance from them stopped; BleepingComputer reports that eMudhra says the affected customer certificates were replaced or migrated, and that the company has not detected malicious use of the keys (eMudhra, Mozilla bug 2083449, 2026-11-10; BleepingComputer, 2026-11-11). eMudhra also decided to exit public TLS, with all issuance from its emSign Root CA - G1 hierarchy to stop before 2026-11-16 and an independent review due 2026-12-04 (eMudhra, Mozilla bug 2083449, 2026-11-10). No page read from Google, Microsoft, Apple, Mozilla or the incident tracker names the G2B or G2C issuers or says a vendor blocked them.

Open finding: eMudhra: the private keys of eight ECDSA intermediate CA certificates were trivially recoverable, so anyone could forge trusted HTTPS certificates, and eight RSA intermediates were revoked on 2026-11-07 for key handling eMudhra cannot show compliant; browsers block them, clients with their own trust store or no revocation checking need an update (CVE-2026-111943 in Go) →

item.title: Plone anonymous RCE chain: update or install the 20261110 hotfix, block portal_modifier, check modifier conditions
item.description: The Plone and Zope security team released fixes on 2026-11-10 for a chain of issues that together let an anonymous visitor run code on the server in Plone 6.0, 6.1 and 6.2 and, per the team, back to at least 4.3; the entry point is a CMFEditions flaw rated 9.8 with no privileges required, and its advisory says a working proof of concept exists. The team's fixes are the updated packages or the hotfix package Products.PloneHotfix20261110, a workaround that blocks URLs containing portal_modifier has applied since the 2026-11-02 pre-announcement, CVE ids are requested and no source reports exploitation.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOA2

Plone security fix of 2026-11-10: a chain of missing security declarations and opened modules lets an anonymous visitor run code on the server in every supported Plone version and back to 4.3; a working proof of concept exists, no CVE ids yet, no exploitation reported

The Plone and Zope security team says the fixes it released on 2026-11-10 close a chain of several issues that together let an anonymous visitor run code on the server, in all supported Plone versions (6.0, 6.1 and 6.2) and in older ones back to at least 4.3 (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10). The anonymous entry point is Products.CMFEditions: the conditional modifiers in portal_modifier had no security declarations, so an anonymous visitor could change a modifier's TALES condition and then run it, and the condition is also evaluated when an editor saves versioned content (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10). Products.CMFPlone, Products.MimetypesRegistry and plone.batching opened whole modules to restricted code, which let TALES expressions and Python scripts escape the sandbox and reach modules such as os, and plone.restapi opened the json module (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10). The CMFEditions advisory rates its flaw 9.8 with no privileges required and states that a working proof of concept exists; the team says details are public and that with current AI tools it may not take long to turn them into a working exploit, and no source reports exploitation (Plone, 2026-11-10; Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10).

The fixed packages are CMFPlone 6.2.3, 6.1.6 and 6.0.16 with the helper package versions the announcement lists, or the hotfix Products.PloneHotfix20261110, which covers Plone 4.3 to 6.2, and all Zope instances must be restarted afterwards (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10). The team's pre-announcement of 2026-11-02 already gave the workaround, to block any URL containing portal_modifier at the web server at any path depth, which only helps if Zope's own port cannot be reached directly; the team advises keeping it after updating (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-02). After the fix, restricted code can import only the names Plone itself needs from the closed modules, so custom scripts that import others now get an Unauthorized error (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10).

Exposure
Any Plone site reachable by anonymous visitors, on a version below the fixed packages; no source states a non-default setting that the anonymous path needs, and Plone 5.2 and older are out of security support, with the fix released as an exception.
Detection
Web-server access logs for anonymous requests whose path contains portal_modifier; and the stored state, which survives the update: a changed modifier condition stays in the database, so as Manager open @@check-modifier-conditions on the site root, or read the hotfix's startup log line that reports modified versioning conditions, and treat the server as compromised if a condition is not recognised, although defaults have changed over time so a difference alone is not an attack (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10).
Defender takeaway
Update or install the hotfix and restart now on every internet-facing Plone site, keep the portal_modifier block in place, and run the modifier-condition check afterwards, because the fix does not remove a condition an anonymous request already stored.

item.title: Apache httpd mod_http2 RCE: update to 2.4.71 or drop h2/h2c from Protocols; Debian, Ubuntu, Alpine fixed
item.description: The Apache HTTP Server project released 2.4.71 on 2026-11-11 to fix CVE-2026-119618, a race in mod_http2 that it rates critical and says can lead to remote code execution in versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70; Red Hat adds that it is unauthenticated, affects only servers with HTTP/2 enabled through the Protocols directive, and that public research has demonstrated a reliable exploit, while no source reports exploitation. Red Hat has fixed RHEL 9 and 10, Debian bookworm and trixie and Alpine ship 2.4.71 packages, Ubuntu has shipped backported fixes, while a researcher's public test reproduces crashes on 2.4.70 and, per Wordfence, does not show code execution.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-119618updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-119618, Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55 to 2.4.70: a race in mod_http2 assign_headers() corrupts heap memory and leads to remote code execution on servers with HTTP/2 enabled; fixed in 2.4.71, Red Hat calls it unauthenticated and claims public exploit research, no exploitation reported

Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71, released on 2026-11-11, fixes CVE-2026-119618, a race in mod_http2's assign_headers() that the project rates critical and says can lead to remote code execution, in versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 (Apache HTTP Server project, 2026-11-11). The project publishes no CVSS score; Red Hat scores it CVSS 3.1 9.8 and says it allows unauthenticated remote code execution, with a worker thread writing into memory owned by the connection thread through a shared lock-free allocator (Red Hat Product Security, 2026-11-11). Red Hat states that only servers with HTTP/2 (h2 or h2c) enabled through the Protocols directive are affected and that HTTP/1.1-only servers are not (Red Hat Product Security, 2026-11-11); the project's own page is silent on that prerequisite (Apache HTTP Server project, 2026-11-11).

On exploitation the sources differ. Wiz wrote at its publication that no exploit was available and no exploitation in the wild was reported (Wiz, 2026-11-11), while Red Hat says public research has demonstrated a reliable exploit against a default-configured server with mod_http2 enabled, without linking it (Red Hat Product Security, 2026-11-11). A researcher has since posted a test setup that reports memory corruption and Apache child-process crashes on 2.4.70, and Wordfence says it does not demonstrate remote command execution (Wordfence, 2026-11-12). No source reports attacks, and the project's advisory carries no exploitation or workaround statement (Apache HTTP Server project, 2026-11-11). Wiz advises disabling HTTP/2 temporarily as the interim measure (Wiz, 2026-11-11).

The upstream fix is 2.4.71. The project lists standalone mod_h2 releases from GitHub, 2.0.8 through 2.0.42, as affected and names no fixed standalone release (Apache HTTP Server project, 2026-11-11). Red Hat shipped mod_http2 errata for RHEL 9 (mod_http2-2.0.26-7.el9_9.1) and RHEL 10 (mod_http2-2.0.29-5.el10_3.1) on 2026-11-11, rates them Important (Red Hat, 2026-11-11; Red Hat, 2026-11-11), says the packages allocate each HTTP/2 stream from a separate allocator, which makes exploitation substantially more complex, and lists RHEL 8 and earlier as not affected (Red Hat Product Security, 2026-11-11); Debian's tracker lists apache2 2.4.71-1~deb12u1 for bookworm (DLA-4902-1) and 2.4.71-1~deb13u1 for trixie (DSA-6620-1) as fixed while forky is still vulnerable (Debian Security Tracker, 2026-11-13), Ubuntu's USN-9090-1 fixes 22.04 LTS to 26.10, and 20.04 LTS through ESM (Ubuntu, 2026-11-12), Alpine 3.21 to 3.24 ship 2.4.71-r0 (Alpine Linux, 2026-11-13) and SUSE lists the issue as pending (SUSE, 2026-11-13).

Exposure
An Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55 to 2.4.70, or a distribution mod_http2 build without the vendor's fix, that has the mod_http2 module loaded and h2 or h2c in a Protocols directive for the server or a virtual host; the loaded modules and the Protocols directives of the configuration show it, and the distribution advisory, not the upstream version string, shows whether a backported fix is installed.
Detection
Neither the project nor Red Hat publishes indicators of compromise; the researcher's test shows the corruption as httpd child-process crashes inside the allocator and HTTP/2 stream code (researcher repository, 2026-11-12), so watch for child crashes in the error log; shells or interpreters started by an httpd worker are an inference from the flaw class, not a source statement.
Defender takeaway
Update internet-facing servers that serve HTTP/2 to 2.4.71 or the distribution's fixed package and restart, and where no fix is available yet remove h2 and h2c from Protocols until it is, because Red Hat describes an unauthenticated path and a public exploit while the project describes neither.

A researcher's public test setup reports memory corruption and Apache child-process crashes on 2.4.70 and a clean run on 2.4.71 (researcher repository, 2026-11-12), and Wordfence says it does not demonstrate remote command execution (Wordfence, 2026-11-12); the researcher's results table records crashes inside the allocator and the HTTP/2 stream code in an instrumented build (researcher repository, 2026-11-12), and the same repository lists mod_h2 2.0.43 as the fixed standalone release.
