item.title: ScreenConnect SCKit: second wave hits on-prem; disable RMM+, update technician clients to 26.6.5+
item.description: Huntress saw an operator use access to several cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels on 2026-11-11 to run Run Command as SYSTEM on groups of managed endpoints, installing an attacker-controlled second ScreenConnect client and the SCKit toolkit on at least 288 hosts at 48 organisations within 90 minutes; Sophos independently saw the same client deployments. Huntress later said the activity seems related to the third-party RMM+ extension, whose versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 accepted a blank access key; ConnectWise's CNA record CVE-2026-127063 (CVSS 4.0 9.3) says the extension uses a static API secret by default, names no fix and gives disabling as the mitigation, while a Huntress spokesperson says the panel-access vector is still unclear and Blackpoint calls the extensions' role unresolved. A second wave on 2026-11-13 hit 205 hosts at 41 organisations (Huntress) and appears to target on-premises instances with mitigations pending (Blackpoint); Microsoft describes a rogue client built to deliver a payload to the technician who connects, which ConnectWise says ScreenConnect clients 26.6.5 and later block.
item.content:encoded:
HIGHCVE-2026-127063updatedNATOB1

ScreenConnect: commands pushed through Run Command to at least 288 managed endpoints at 48 Huntress customers within 90 minutes on 2026-11-11 installed a rogue second client and the SCKit toolkit; Huntress links the activity to the RMM+ extension, whose versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 accepted a blank access key

On 2026-11-11 Huntress observed an operator using access to several cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to run commands as SYSTEM on groups of managed endpoints through the Run Command feature, hitting at least 288 hosts at 48 organisations within 90 minutes (Huntress, 2026-11-11). Each host installed an attacker-controlled second client and fetched SCKit, a 16-file toolkit delivered encrypted that sets the legitimate client to manual start so the attacker's copy replaces it and runs a per-host executable from a scheduled task (Huntress, 2026-11-11). A second wave on 2026-11-13 hit 205 hosts at 41 organisations with no follow-on executions observed (Huntress, 2026-11-13), and Blackpoint says it appears to target on-premises instances where mitigations are still pending (Blackpoint, 2026-11-13).

Huntress's later update says the activity seems related to RMM+, a third-party extension that bypasses ScreenConnect's accounts, roles and MFA: versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 accepted a blank access key when an administrator had never set one (Huntress, 2026-11-11). ConnectWise, as CNA, published CVE-2026-127063 (CVSS 4.0 9.3) saying the extension uses a static API secret by default; it names no fixed version, removed the extension from cloud-hosted instances and tells on-premises customers to disable it and not reinstall it (ConnectWise, 2026-11-12).

Microsoft describes the technician stage: RelayTrap, a replacement client compiled on the endpoint with the .NET C# compiler and designed to deliver a payload to the technician who connects, and browser-access code that searches Chrome, Edge and Opera profiles for cookies named .ASPXAUTH, with a component designed to queue payloads through the console's Shared Toolbox (Microsoft, 2026-11-13). ConnectWise says clients 26.6.5 and later block the transfer, and Microsoft adds that a cloud-console update does not update technician clients (Microsoft, 2026-11-13); Huntress and Blackpoint saw no successful technician compromise (Huntress, 2026-11-11; Blackpoint, 2026-11-13).

Exposure
A ScreenConnect instance whose panel can run commands on managed endpoints, run by the organisation or an IT provider; an RMM+ extension at any version, since ConnectWise's record names a static default secret, with versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 and a blank key as the condition Huntress describes; a technician host client older than 26.6.5; an endpoint with a second client service pointing at a foreign relay.
Detection
ScreenConnect instance audit logs, Run Command and Toolbox history for mass executions nobody started and RMM+ requests with no matching login (Huntress, 2026-11-11), and file-transfer-and-run events (event ID 201, per Blackpoint) (Blackpoint, 2026-11-13); process-creation telemetry with the ScreenConnect client service as parent of cmd, PowerShell or msiexec, curl or PowerShell downloads followed by a silent msiexec install (the Sophos pattern) (Sophos, 2026-11-11), a scheduled-task PowerShell watcher that compiles an executable with the .NET compiler (Microsoft, 2026-11-13), and a client service named like a Windows component (Huntress, 2026-11-13).
Defender takeaway
Treat Run Command or Toolbox executions you did not start as a compromise; disable RMM+ and the four other extensions the first notice named, update every technician host client to 26.6.5 or later, rotate ScreenConnect credentials and revoke active sessions and the browser and identity-provider sessions the toolkit could steal, and keep hosts and technician workstations out of service until the rogue client and persistence are gone (Huntress, 2026-11-11; Microsoft, 2026-11-13). Removing the rogue client alone leaves the persistence and the web sessions, and the cleanup script found in the kit must not be used (Microsoft, 2026-11-13).

item.title: Microsoft: GSocket relay clients on exploited Linux web servers survive the patch; hunt the host, not the app
item.description: Microsoft Defender telemetry shows multiple unrelated threat actors deploying GSocket, an open-source remote access tool that connects both ends outbound through a public relay, on Linux servers after exploiting an internet-facing web application, with kernel-thread-like process names and layered persistence through cron, systemd and shell profiles. Because the client runs independently of the exploited application, patching does not remove it, and blocking an address or domain is unlikely to cut off access.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

GSocket on compromised Linux web servers: Microsoft sees several unrelated actors install the open-source relay client after exploiting an internet-facing web application, so access outlives the patch; no inbound listener, no attacker-hosted infrastructure

Microsoft observed several unrelated threat actors deploy GSocket, an open-source remote access tool, on Linux servers after exploiting an internet-facing web application, and says it kept access after the exploited vulnerabilities were remediated (Microsoft, 2026-11-11). The chain starts with command execution as a child of the web server or application runtime, where curl fetches an installation script that bash runs; the script profiles the host, picks a client matching the architecture, stages it as a hidden, executable file in a writable or memory-backed path such as /dev/shm and opens encrypted outbound command and control through the Global Socket Relay Network (Microsoft, 2026-11-11). The client is then disguised with kernel-thread-like process names (bash exec -a), persisted through cron, systemd units, shell profiles, watchdogs and redundant copies, and the staging files are removed (Microsoft, 2026-11-11). In a few incidents the actors afterwards attempted the Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-43284, known as Dirty Frag, to reach root; Microsoft gives no success statement and no affected or fixed versions (Microsoft, 2026-11-11).

Both the compromised host and the operator connect outbound to the public relay, so the host needs no inbound listener, inbound firewall rules do not see the traffic and a shared secret, not an address, pairs the endpoints, which lets the operator reconnect later from any compatible client; Microsoft therefore says that blocking an address or domain is unlikely to cut off access, while egress filtering and outbound monitoring can see it (Microsoft, 2026-11-11). Microsoft's telemetry is concentrated on web applications and hosting; education and research and technology and telecommunications were the largest shares of affected organisations, which Microsoft says reflect exposure more likely than deliberate sector selection (Microsoft, 2026-11-11).

Exposure
Any Linux web, CMS or hosting server whose internet-facing application was exploited, patched or not, in the months before the patch; Microsoft says the same persistence problem applies when initial access came through remote access services or cloud shell sessions.
Detection
Process-creation telemetry with parent lineage, where a web-server or application-runtime process starts curl and then bash, followed by a long-lived process whose name imitates a kernel thread but whose executable sits in a hidden or memory-backed path; file events in /dev/shm and /tmp; new cron entries and systemd units with plausible service names created in the same window as the download; shell startup file changes; and long-lived outbound sessions to a public relay from servers that have no reason to initiate them. After patching, remove the client, its persistence and staged files, and verify that the outbound relay connections stopped, because persistence is layered and stopping the process alone does not remove access (Microsoft, 2026-11-11).

Triage: Microsoft notes that the same relay model also serves legitimate remote administration, and says a match must be judged on process ancestry, execution context, persistence changes and related network activity; a client started from a web-service process tree, from a writable or memory-backed path and under a kernel-thread-like name is the pattern it describes (Microsoft, 2026-11-11).

Defender takeaway
Treat every Linux web server whose application was exploited as possibly holding a relay client, not only web shells, and hunt it on the host after patching; Microsoft's hardening steps are deny-by-default egress with monitoring of relay connections, non-executable mounts for temporary and memory-backed directories, and a review of cron entries, systemd units and shell startup files.

item.title: Unit 42: Falcon C2 runs inside the browser, fed by a script tag in government webmail such as Roundcube
item.description: Unit 42 describes Falcon, a NodeJS command-and-control framework whose JavaScript implant runs inside the victim's browser and leaves no file on the endpoint, planted by a script tag in government webmail portals and web applications, among them the Roundcube webmail of a Middle Eastern foreign ministry (39 instances in that country), and by a sideloaded Chrome extension disguised as a PDF viewer. Unit 42 saw it against government bodies in one Middle Eastern and four Southeast Asian countries between March and May 2026, names no actor, does not say how the script tags were placed and is unaware how the extensions are deployed, and assesses with high confidence that Falcon and PeckBirdy are variants of one core framework.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

Falcon: Unit 42 describes a browser-resident command-and-control framework planted in government webmail and web applications, with a script tag in Roundcube at a Middle Eastern foreign ministry and a sideloaded 'PDF Viewer' extension elsewhere; it shares its core with PeckBirdy

Unit 42 describes Falcon C2, also called XG and not the CrowdStrike Falcon sensor, a NodeJS command-and-control framework whose operator-controlled JavaScript implant runs inside the victim's browser, so the endpoint holds no file for it (Unit 42, 2026-11-11). A script tag placed in a trusted site makes each visit request the implant from the Falcon server, which returns a script obfuscated per browser session, and the implant then holds a TLS WebSocket to the server while the tab is open and runs operator JavaScript through eval (Unit 42, 2026-11-11). Unit 42 identified compromised government entities in one Middle Eastern and four Southeast Asian countries between March and May 2026, among them ministries and law enforcement agencies, and names no actor (Unit 42, 2026-11-11).

In April 2026 a script tag inserted into the Roundcube webmail portal of a Middle Eastern ministry of foreign affairs let the operator intercept credentials as users signed in and monitor sessions (39 Roundcube instances in that country, none observed elsewhere; how the tag got in is not stated) (Unit 42, 2026-11-11). In May 2026 a module in a Southeast Asian police web application harvested usernames and then showed a fake Adobe Flash Player update prompt to chosen users, which served the Antino implant that uses Microsoft OneDrive for command and control (Unit 42, 2026-11-11). Against a justice-department entity in another country, a Chrome extension named PDF Viewer, sideloaded in developer mode, checked in every 3 to 4 minutes for over three weeks and exfiltrated plaintext credentials for an internal correspondence system and a screenshot of a document the victim was viewing (Unit 42, 2026-11-11). The Jewelbug campaign also used an extension named PDF Viewer (Symantec, 2026-08-13); Unit 42 lists it only as a further resource.

Unit 42 assesses with high confidence that Falcon and PeckBirdy (Trend's JScript framework used by China-aligned actors since 2023) are variants of one core framework; that is code lineage, not who operates Falcon (Unit 42, 2026-11-11; Trend Micro, 2026-01-26).

Exposure
Internal webmail, ticketing and case-management portals whose templates or headers an attacker can edit (Roundcube is the named case), and managed Chrome browsers that allow extensions to be sideloaded in developer mode; Unit 42 does not say how the script tags or the extensions reached their targets.
Detection
Unit 42's four monitoring items, telemetry class first: template and header integrity on webmail, ticketing and case-management portals for a script tag loading a resource from an unfamiliar domain, especially one returning a heavily numeric JavaScript array with a small decoder loop; extension inventory for developer-mode extensions imitating utilities such as PDF viewers with broad permissions; Baidu Analytics-style cookie or local-storage keys on internal government web applications; and OneDrive traffic to tenants outside the organisation's own with repeated small JSON writes (Unit 42, 2026-11-11).

Triage: Unit 42's basis for the cookie check is that Baidu Analytics cookies are normal on sites that use that service and anomalous on internal government web applications where it has no reason to appear (Unit 42, 2026-11-11).

Defender takeaway
Compare the templates and headers of internal webmail and case-management portals with a known-good copy and list every external script source they load, and inventory the Chrome extensions installed in developer mode on managed browsers; a browser-resident implant leaves nothing on the endpoint for file-based tools to find.

item.title: CCB: attackers signed in to Entra ID with an SMS code alone; turn off SMS first-factor sign-in
item.description: Belgium's Centre for Cybersecurity warned on 2026-11-10 that a trusted partner observed successful attacks against multiple Belgian organisations in which attackers abused Microsoft Entra ID SMS first-factor sign-in, where a phone number and a one-time code replace the password. The warning gives no victim count, actor, date range or attack chain and says nothing on how the codes were obtained; the CCB's priority step is to find who uses SMS sign-in, give them an alternative and disable it.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOA2

Belgium's CCB warns that attackers abused Microsoft Entra ID SMS first-factor sign-in (phone number and one-time code, no password) to compromise several Belgian organisations; turning off 'Use for sign-in' is the priority step

The Belgian Centre for Cybersecurity (CCB) warned on 2026-11-10 that a trusted partner had observed successful attacks against multiple Belgian organisations in which attackers abused Microsoft Entra ID SMS as a first factor, the sign-in mode in which a phone number and a one-time code replace the password (CCB, 2026-11-10). The warning gives no victim count, sector, actor, date range or attack chain, and it does not say how the codes were obtained; its only statement on the factor itself is that SMS and voice can be phished, intercepted or SIM-swapped (CCB, 2026-11-10). No other source reports the Belgian attacks. Microsoft describes the method as designed for frontline workers, advises enabling it only for them, and says it is different from SMS as a multifactor method, which needs a username and password (Microsoft Learn, 2026-10-30). Microsoft is disabling first-factor sign-in in tenants with no such traffic in the previous 30 days (Microsoft Learn, 2026-10-30) and retires its own SMS and voice delivery on 2027-02-01 for all users except Global Administrators and external users, who follow on 2027-07-01; a customer-configured telephony provider can keep the methods working (Microsoft Learn, 2026-09-23).

Exposure
An Entra tenant whose SMS authentication method policy has first-factor sign-in turned on for any user or group; the CCB's path is Authentication methods, SMS, "Use for sign-in", and the Authentication methods activity report shows who actually uses it (CCB, 2026-11-10). Microsoft's how-to calls the same setting "Enable first factor sign-in" and says that leaving it unchecked limits SMS to multifactor authentication and self-service password reset (Microsoft Learn, 2026-10-30).
Detection
In Entra sign-in logs, look for successful sign-ins that used SMS as the authentication method; in audit logs, for phone-number or authentication-method changes; then for unusual locations or devices and follow-on mailbox rules or application consents, reviewing as far back as log retention allows (CCB, 2026-11-10).
Defender takeaway
Disable SMS first-factor sign-in now for everyone who has an alternative and restrict it to the smallest group where it must stay, as the CCB advises; remove SMS and voice for privileged accounts only after each has a working phishing-resistant method, and avoid a blind switch-off, which can lock users out or leave them with a password alone (CCB, 2026-11-10). Microsoft's own clearing reaches only tenants with no first-factor SMS sign-in traffic in the previous 30 days (Microsoft Learn, 2026-10-30), so a tenant that uses the method stays exposed until it acts.

Veeam's KB4966 of 2026-11-10 adds the Veeam Software and Infrastructure Appliances, workers, Linux-based helper appliances and recovery media to the affected products, with the fixed CIQ kernel delivered through Veeam Updater since 2026-11-02 and a private fix for helper appliances managed from Windows servers; Ubuntu's tracker now lists the generic 22.04, 24.04 and 26.04 LTS kernels as fixed while 20.04 and older and some variant kernels remain in progress, and the body states again that the CNA and upstream score the flaw differently.

item.title: Update: eMudhra: eight ECDSA CA keys guessable, eight RSA CAs revoked; Windows drops the rest 2026-11-16; update clients
item.description: SonicWall's advisory of 2026-11-10 says SonicOS firewalls with Client DPI-SSL enabled kept trusting the compromised eMudhra chains and re-signed them for clients; fixed in SonicOS 7.3.4-7015 (Gen7) and 8.2.3-8015 (Gen8), so a Gen7 unit on 7.3.4-7013 is still affected. Apple's macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 and 15.8.3 now block the certificates in the command-line tools, Microsoft removes the remaining eMudhra roots from Windows, Edge and WebView2 from 2026-11-16, and Cisco's advisory is at version 1.9.
item.content:encoded:
Update11 Nov 2026 03:55 UTCrun 2026-11-11T0256Z-intelsummaryentitiesaffected_productssourcesevidenceactionsbodyheadlinesourcing_note

SonicWall's advisory of 2026-11-10 says SonicOS firewalls with Client DPI-SSL enabled kept trusting the compromised eMudhra chains and re-signed them for clients; fixed in SonicOS 7.3.4-7015 (Gen7) and 8.2.3-8015 (Gen8), so a Gen7 unit on 7.3.4-7013 is still affected. Apple's macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 and 15.8.3 now block the certificates in the command-line tools, Microsoft removes the remaining eMudhra roots from Windows, Edge and WebView2 from 2026-11-16, and Cisco's advisory is at version 1.9.

SonicWall's informational advisory SNWLID-2026-0021 of 2026-11-10, which has no CVE and no workaround, says SonicOS appliances with Client DPI-SSL enabled continued to trust certificate chains issued by the compromised eMudhra intermediate CAs because the firewall's local certificate store trusted the underlying roots, and that the firewall then re-signed traffic from the impacted servers with its local DPI-SSL CA certificate, preventing client browsers from rejecting connections signed by the untrusted intermediates (SonicWall, 2026-11-10; SonicWall advisory data, 2026-11-10). SonicWall removed the affected root certificates from the SonicOS certificate store and added blocking logic for the compromised chain. Affected are Gen7 hardware firewalls (TZ 270 to TZ 670, NSa 2700 to 6700, NSsp 10700 to 15700) and Gen7 NSv up to 7.3.4-7013, fixed in 7.3.4-7015 and higher, and Gen8 hardware (TZ 80 to TZ 680, NSa 2800 to 5800) and Gen8 NSv up to 8.2.2-8015, fixed in 8.2.3-8015 and higher; a Gen7 firewall that took only 7.3.4-7013 is therefore still affected (SonicWall, 2026-11-10).

Apple revised its support page on 2026-11-10: from macOS 27.2.1 the command-line tools no longer accept the twelve intermediate certificates, and the two roots they chain to, with three more eMudhra roots, leave /etc/ssl/cert.pem; macOS 26.7.3 and 15.8.3 carry the same protection, and after updating the manual removal need not be repeated (Apple, 2026-11-10). The revised page no longer carries the block dates of its 2026-10-30 version, so the 2026-10-22 date of the tracker and BleepingComputer stands for Apple's block.

Microsoft's post carries an update of 2026-11-10: the remaining eMudhra roots leave Microsoft products starting 2026-11-16, the ten remaining roots leave the Windows trusted root list through the automatic certificate-trust update, Edge and WebView2 drop default trust for emSign Root CA - G1, C1, ECC Root CA and Root TLS CA - G1 on the same date, Azure Linux images follow that day, and the .NET container images and the Microsoft Build of OpenJDK follow upstream releases (Microsoft, 2026-11-10). Cisco's advisory is at version 1.9 of 2026-11-10, which updates the products under investigation, impacted and not impacted (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-11-10).

Open finding: eMudhra: the private keys of eight ECDSA intermediate CA certificates were trivially recoverable, so anyone could forge trusted HTTPS certificates, and eight RSA intermediates were revoked on 2026-11-07 for key handling eMudhra cannot show compliant; browsers block them, clients with their own trust store or no revocation checking need an update (CVE-2026-111943 in Go) →

item.description: PK Softech and the State Secretariat for Security Policy said on 2026-11-10 that no concrete ransom demand reached the supplier or the federal bodies, that the supplier never contacted the attackers, that the Confederation paid nothing and that there is still no indication of publication on the darkweb, which qualifies the press report that Akira demands ransom.

PK Softech and the State Secretariat for Security Policy said on 2026-11-10 that no concrete ransom demand reached the supplier or the federal bodies, that the supplier never contacted the attackers, that the Confederation paid nothing and that there is still no indication of publication on the darkweb, which qualifies the press report that Akira demands ransom.

item.title: Update: Danfoss AK-SM 800A: six unpatched pre-auth RCE flaws, Strict mode does not remove them; France blames IRGC
item.description: BACS published its own public warning on 2026-11-10: it says Switzerland is affected and that the controllers also run in butchers, restaurants, pharmacies, doctors' practices, laboratories, logistics, industry and farms, many of whose operators do not know their plants are reachable from the internet, and it repeats that security updates for the AK-SM 800A and 8xxA family exist and that newer firmware enforces HTTPS.
item.content:encoded:
Update11 Nov 2026 03:52 UTCrun 2026-11-11T0256Z-intelsummarysourcesevidencebody

BACS published its own public warning on 2026-11-10: it says Switzerland is affected and that the controllers also run in butchers, restaurants, pharmacies, doctors' practices, laboratories, logistics, industry and farms, many of whose operators do not know their plants are reachable from the internet, and it repeats that security updates for the AK-SM 800A and 8xxA family exist and that newer firmware enforces HTTPS.

BACS published a public warning on 2026-11-10, which repeats the earlier warning of the Cyber Security Hub advisory cited above; it says the attacks of recent weeks show that Switzerland is affected too and that it is repeating its warning because the systems are widespread among small and medium-sized businesses (translated from German) (BACS, 2026-11-10). Per BACS, attackers reach management interfaces that are directly reachable from the internet and then change temperatures, defrost cycles, alarm thresholds or notification settings remotely, which can spoil food, medicines and other temperature-sensitive goods; it names the end-of-life AK-SM 800 and AK-SC 355, the current AK-SM 800A and 8xxA family when it runs outdated firmware, and Copeland and Dixell XWEB.

What is new is the wider population: BACS lists butchers and food producers, restaurants and hotels, pharmacies, doctors' practices and laboratories, logistics and warehouses, industry and farms among the users, many of which do not know their cooling plants are reachable from the internet or run by an external provider, and it repeats what the Hub advisory already said, that security updates fixing the known flaws are available for the AK-SM 800A and 8xxA family and that newer firmware activates additional protections and enforces encrypted HTTPS communication (translated from German) (BACS, 2026-11-10). It recommends identifying the controllers, those run by contractors included, installing vendor updates, restricting unsupported systems to trusted networks or a VPN, reaching them remotely only through one centrally managed access point with default passwords replaced, and replacing end-of-life products; it names no attacker, no exploited CVE and no count of Swiss victims.

Open finding: Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb refrigeration controllers compromised in France, six more European countries and Switzerland, with France blaming the IRGC unit Shahid Kaveh for the October campaign; Midnight Blue reports six unpatched pre-authentication flaws in AK-SM 800A firmware up to 5.3.2 →

item.title: Stolen Qubole vendor credentials assumed customers' idle AWS integration roles; a source-IP condition stops it
item.description: Wiz, working with Sentra and Mandiant, reports that between 2026-10-14 and 2026-10-26 an actor used IAM credentials from an AWS account associated with the data platform Qubole to assume customers' cross-account integration roles, each call carrying the correct External ID; most roles had otherwise been idle. Inside each account the actor listed resources, read Secrets Manager, Parameter Store and Lambda configuration, tested harvested AWS, Entra ID and Okta credentials with TruffleHog and downloaded S3 data, in some cases whole buckets; no victim is named, the counts range from more than a dozen to dozens, and how the vendor identities were compromised is not known.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB1

Qubole: an attacker used IAM credentials from a vendor-associated AWS account to assume dormant cross-account integration roles in dozens of customer accounts, then harvested secrets and validated Entra ID and Okta client credentials (Wiz and Sentra, 14 to 26 October)

Wiz, working with Sentra and Mandiant, observed a threat actor using IAM credentials from an AWS account associated with Qubole, a big-data platform, between 2026-10-14 and 2026-10-26 (Wiz, 2026-11-09). The actor used two Qubole IAM users to call sts:AssumeRole on the cross-account integration roles that customers had created to trust Qubole's account; "every AssumeRole request we attributed to the threat actor included an External ID, and every one succeeded", most of the roles were otherwise not in use, and the traffic came from a rented hosting server and commercial VPN exits, not the AWS infrastructure where legitimate platform traffic originates (Wiz, 2026-11-09; Sentra, 2026-11-09).

Inside each account the actor enumerated resources, read Lambda function configuration, Secrets Manager and Systems Manager Parameter Store, ran TruffleHog to test AWS access keys, Entra ID service-principal client secrets and Okta client credentials it found, and then downloaded S3 data opportunistically, in some cases whole buckets in one session (Wiz, 2026-11-09). Wiz found no tie to other reported activity and judges the targeting opportunistic; how the Qubole IAM users were compromised is not stated. Sentra writes that dozens of Qubole customers were impacted, and BleepingComputer could not find a public Qubole announcement (Sentra, 2026-11-09; BleepingComputer, 2026-11-10). No Swiss or public-sector victim is named, but the exposure is shared by any account that gave a data or analytics vendor a cross-account role and left it in place.

Exposure
Any AWS account holding an IAM role whose trust policy lets a Qubole account, or any other vendor account, assume it, including roles left from integrations that ended; the roles' trust policies and last-used data show them, and Wiz publishes the vendor account identifier, the two principals and the attacker address ranges for a CloudTrail hunt back to 2026-10-01 (Wiz, 2026-11-09).
Detection
In cloud control-plane audit logs, AssumeRole events into integration roles whose calling identity is the vendor account but whose source address is not AWS infrastructure, and session names with a consistent attacker-chosen prefix; GetCallerIdentity calls from many keys within seconds and Entra ID or Okta sign-ins by service principals or clients right after, as the actor validates credentials; ListSecrets, GetSecretValue, Parameter Store and Lambda configuration reads in bursts. Object reads are absent from CloudTrail management events, so S3 data events or server access logs must be on, and Wiz says missing logs left responders unable to see what was read (Wiz, 2026-11-09).

Triage: legitimate vendor traffic comes from the vendor's own AWS infrastructure; the correct External ID does not discriminate, because it is logged in plaintext and often stored by the vendor, while a vendor role assumed from a consumer VPN or a hosting provider the vendor has never used is the high-signal case.

Defender takeaway
Inventory third-party trust relationships, delete the roles of ended integrations, narrow each trusted principal to the vendor's specific principal and add a source-address or endpoint condition, which Wiz says alone would have blocked every observed assumption; after an incident, revoke the issued role sessions and rotate every secret, parameter, Lambda variable and identity-provider credential the role could read.

item.title: Insikt: GhostFrame implant re-disables ESXi execInstalledOnly every five seconds and steals guest credentials
item.description: Recorded Future's Insikt Group describes GhostFrame, a command-and-control and post-exploitation framework for VMware ESXi hosts that operators must already hold root on: its vmhostd-core implant persists through ESXi boot scripts, disables the ESXi firewall and the execInstalledOnly control about every five seconds, and a web panel controls guest VMs and runs VMkatz against memory snapshots and virtual disks to recover Windows credentials. Insikt links it to TAG-218, whose activity overlaps Settra ransomware and whose servers targeted SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks and Fortinet VPN appliances in the US and Europe from late August to October 2026.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

GhostFrame: Recorded Future's Insikt Group finds an ESXi post-exploitation framework (vmhostd-core implant, VM control panel, VMkatz credential theft) used by TAG-218, whose activity overlaps Settra ransomware and which targeted SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks and Fortinet VPN appliances in the US and Europe

Insikt Group describes GhostFrame, a previously undocumented command-and-control and post-exploitation framework for compromised VMware ESXi hosts, which it saw used by TAG-218, a group "whose operations overlap with Settra ransomware" (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). Operators must already hold root on the host: the implant, an ELF named vmhostd-core generated from a web operator panel, does not exploit a vulnerability to gain access (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). It copies itself to /opt/vmhostd-core, edits the ESXi boot script /etc/rc.local.d/local.sh and runs /sbin/auto-backup.sh to keep the change across reboots, masquerades as vmhostd (resembling VMware's vmware-hostd), and about every five seconds disables the ESXi firewall and the execInstalledOnly control that restricts execution of unsigned binaries, so an administrator who re-enables them is undone (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). Its command channel opens simultaneous TCP connections to one address on ports 53, 2222, 3389, 4444, 8443 and 9443, keeps the first that succeeds and retries after a random delay of 5 to 12 seconds, which Insikt notes is a network detection opportunity; the implant is mainly an in-memory shellcode loader with a reverse-shell fallback.

From the hypervisor the panel can list registered VMs, change power state, create or delete snapshots, enable VNC on a guest, run a SOCKS5 proxy for pivoting, intercept ESXi logins, and run the open-source VMkatz against VM memory snapshots, virtual disks or whole datastores to recover NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets, SAM and LSA secrets and NTDS.dit data without running anything inside the guest (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). Insikt ties TAG-218's victim-facing servers to VPN-appliance targeting across the US and Europe between late August and October 2026, "predominantly SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks, and Fortinet devices", and says four of those organisations later appeared on the Settra leak site; it assesses that other financially motivated actors are highly likely to adopt the framework, which is an assessment, not an observation (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). Unit 42 independently reports that after CVE-2026-0257 exploitation attackers pivot from the VPN gateway directly to the virtualization layer (Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, 2026-10-20).

Exposure
ESXi hosts whose root credentials, SSH or shell, or vCenter are reachable after an edge compromise; no ESXi vulnerability is involved, so patching ESXi does not address it, and an estate that runs both a SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks or Fortinet VPN appliance and ESXi without isolated hypervisor management is in the pattern Insikt describes.
Detection
In ESXi file-integrity and shell-audit telemetry, changes to local.sh, a process masquerading as the host daemon or an unexpected executable under /opt, and repeated firewall-off and execInstalledOnly resets; in network telemetry, six near-simultaneous SYNs from the hypervisor management address to one destination on those ports, and any outbound command-style traffic from a hypervisor at all; in vCenter and ESXi logs, snapshot creation or deletion, VNC enablement and power-state changes outside change windows; in datastore telemetry, reads of VM memory-snapshot and virtual-disk files by an identity that is not the backup service.

Triage: administrators legitimately edit local.sh, create snapshots and use VNC; the discriminators are a firewall-off and execInstalledOnly loop, a binary under /opt named vmhostd where the genuine daemon is vmware-hostd, and snapshot-file reads by a non-backup account.

Defender takeaway
Treat a VPN-appliance compromise as a possible hypervisor compromise and check the ESXi persistence files and the execInstalledOnly state before declaring the incident closed; restrict ESXi and vCenter management to dedicated administration hosts.

item.title: ESET: Turla's Cereal runs the victim's own Exchange server as C2 and wraps transport agents to collect mail
item.description: ESET found a previously undocumented .NET toolset, Cereal, on a Kazakh government organisation's Exchange server in November 2025 and on a Romanian government organisation's from December 2025, and attributes it to Turla with high confidence. The compromised Exchange server is the command channel, answering requests on web paths that imitate Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover and ActiveSync, and a module injected into the transport service wraps existing transport agents to collect mail, in Romania configured to select messages to or from NATO and EU addresses; ESET could not determine the initial access method.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

Turla's Cereal toolset turns a compromised on-premises Exchange server into the command channel and mail collector at Kazakh and Romanian government bodies, with no attacker infrastructure and no new transport agent registered (ESET)

ESET found a previously undocumented .NET toolset, Cereal, on a Kazakh government organisation's Exchange server on 2025-11-28 and, after tuning its detections, on a Romanian government organisation's Exchange server compromised from 2025-12-23; in Romania the mail-collection module was configured to identify messages to or from NATO and EU institutional addresses (ESET Research, 2026-11-10). ESET attributes Cereal to Turla with high confidence, on the concurrent use of another component publicly linked to Turla and conceptual similarity to older Turla malware, and could not determine the initial access method, although it considers a vulnerability exploit possible because the servers are reachable from the internet (ESET Research, 2026-11-10).

The command channel is the victim's own Exchange server. CerealNeuron runs on the compromised server and passively waits for requests on web paths made to look like Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover and ActiveSync traffic; a correctly encrypted request is treated as a command and a bad one gets a normal-looking Exchange error page, and ESET found no operator-controlled server and could not identify ingress addresses (ESET Research, 2026-11-10). CerealHermit is a network-less variant that reads encrypted command files from disk, and each task runs as a small .NET assembly inside a CerealRunner (mailbox retrieval, Active Directory and WMI queries, LSA secrets extraction, file operations) (ESET Research, 2026-11-10). CerealLoader, the only component written to disk in recognisable .NET form, abuses .NET VTable fixups so native code runs before managed code and is placed where trusted processes load it: the System32 wbem directory (ncobjapi.dll, wbemcomn.dll, loaded by WMI) and the .NET native image cache (ESET Research, 2026-11-10). CerealBox, injected into EdgeTransport.exe, wraps the handlers of transport agents already loaded, so "no new agent appears anywhere in Exchange's configuration"; it keeps messages with .doc, .docx or .pdf attachments that match hard-coded sender, recipient, subject or attachment-name lists and stages them compressed and encrypted on disk for exfiltration through CerealNeuron (ESET Research, 2026-11-10).

Exposure
Any organisation that runs Microsoft Exchange on premises with a role reachable from the internet; ESET names no vulnerable version, so exposure is the deployment model.
Detection
File-integrity telemetry on the Exchange host for DLLs in the System32 wbem directory and .NET native image cache files that do not match the Microsoft originals; module telemetry for non-Microsoft assemblies loaded into EdgeTransport.exe while Get-TransportAgent lists nothing new; web-server logs for requests to the Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover and ActiveSync look-alike paths from clients with no matching mailbox flow, whose encrypted bodies return a generic error page; and Exchange Web Services mailbox retrievals made from the server's own context. With no external C2 and no known entry vector, the check is a compromise assessment of every internet-facing Exchange server.

Triage: third-party anti-spam, data-loss-prevention and archiving products also inject into the transport service, but they are vendor-signed and appear in the transport-agent configuration, which CerealBox does not; the native image cache regenerates legitimately after .NET updates, so a changed timestamp alone is weak, while a file that does not match the Microsoft binary is the signal.

Defender takeaway
Treat internet-facing Exchange servers as top-tier assets with endpoint detection and restricted egress, baseline the wbem directory and the native image cache, and run the compromise assessment now, because network-only detection will not find a channel that rides the victim's own web paths.
